clue.text: Because Charles Ryder does this, we have a novel

definitions.text: Because Charles Ryder does this, we have a novel

parts.words: Because Charles Ryder does this, we have a novel
parts.note: Evelyn Waugh's narrator Charles Ryder goes back to a great country house, and that return gives the novel its title

explanation.surface: A reader muses that one character's habit is the whole reason a famous novel exists.
explanation.walkthrough: Waugh's novel is Brideshead Revisited: its title says what Ryder does to Brideshead.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title describes Ryder going back to a place he once knew, which is what the verb means.

clue.text: Baby food fashionable with founder of Guild of St George

definitions.text: founder of Guild of St George

parts.note: a rusk is a hard biscuit given to teething infants
in means in fashion

explanation.surface: A Victorian founder is pictured improbably alongside trendy food for infants.
explanation.walkthrough: John Ruskin, the Victorian critic, founded the Guild of St George in 1871.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian art critic John Ruskin set up that utopian guild in 1871.

clue.text: Charles Cotton's travelling companion

parts.note: in Cotton's second part of The Compleat Angler the angler Piscator walks with a traveller whose name is the Latin word for wayfarer

explanation.surface: A question about who journeyed with a seventeenth-century poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Cotton wrote the second part of Walton's Compleat Angler, a dialogue between Piscator and a traveller.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for a wayfarer is the name of the walker in Cotton's angling dialogue.

clue.text: Gardener-poet: sonnets he produced

indicators.note: the poems are produced, so the letters of those two words are reworked into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A poet who also gardened is credited with writing some sonnets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produced' rearranges SONNETS HE. William Shenstone was an eighteenth-century poet famous for his landscape garden, The Leasowes.
explanation.definitionFit: William Shenstone wrote verse and laid out the celebrated Leasowes estate, a pioneer of landscape gardening.

clue.text: Johnson said that if a man is tired of London, he suffers from this

definitions.text: Johnson said that if a man is tired of London, he suffers from this

parts.words: Johnson said that if a man is tired of London, he suffers from this
parts.note: Samuel Johnson's remark ends 'he is tired of life', and the Latin phrase for weariness of life names that condition

explanation.surface: A recollection of Samuel Johnson's famous saying about weariness with London.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson told Boswell that a man tired of London is tired of life; the Latin term for that weariness is what is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means weariness of life, exactly the state Johnson diagnosed.

clue.text: He had his day, thanks to Frederick Forsyth

definitions.text: He had his day, thanks to Frederick Forsyth

parts.words: He had his day, thanks to Frederick Forsyth
parts.note: Forsyth's thriller is The Day of the ___, named after its assassin

explanation.surface: Someone enjoyed brief fame courtesy of a thriller writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had his day' sounds like a fading star, but points to Forsyth's novel The Day of the Jackal.
explanation.definitionFit: The assassin's codename gives Forsyth's thriller its title, so his 'day' belongs to that animal name.

clue.text: Cronin's was of sixpence

parts.note: A. J. Cronin wrote a novel whose title borrows from the nursery rhyme 'Sing ... of sixpence'

explanation.surface: A remark that a novelist's something was worth only sixpence.
explanation.walkthrough: A. J. Cronin's 1964 novel is A Song of Sixpence, from the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: The first words of Cronin's novel title, borrowed from the rhyme, complete the phrase in the clue.

clue.text: Ken really loses his right to author Passenger

indicators.note: the words Ken really lose a letter, so something is taken away from them

explanation.surface: A man called Ken forfeits his entitlement to write a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right' sounds like an entitlement but is just R. Thomas Keneally, the Australian novelist, wrote Passenger (1979).
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Keneally, the Australian novelist of Schindler's Ark, published the novel Passenger in 1979.

clue.text: Secure deer for castigator of the "Cockney School"

parts.note: to lock is to make fast or secure
a hart is a male red deer

explanation.surface: Protecting a stag is linked to a critic of Keats and Hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: J. G. Lockhart attacked Keats, Leigh Hunt and others as the 'Cockney School' in Blackwood's Magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gibson Lockhart wrote the Blackwood's articles deriding Keats and Hunt as the Cockney School of poetry.

clue.text: Laureate's water at high temperature (35)

parts.note: the sea is a body of water
a fever is a raised body temperature

explanation.surface: A poet laureate's bathwater turns out to be too hot.
explanation.walkthrough: John Masefield, Poet Laureate, wrote the poem Sea-Fever ('I must go down to the seas again').
explanation.definitionFit: Sea-Fever is the best-known poem by John Masefield, who held the post of Poet Laureate.

clue.text: Spirit of French town Is study included in symbols?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held reads 'Spirit of French town Is study included in symbols?': the words of 12-across's clue are run onto it, so the clue as printed is not available
annotationWithheld.clue: Spirit of French town Is study included in symbols?

clue.text: Shan't airline somehow represent Shakespearean curate?

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters of those two words are rearranged in some way

explanation.surface: A question about whether an airline will refuse to act for a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges SHANT AIRLINE. Sir Nathaniel is the curate in Love's Labour's Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: In Love's Labour's Lost the pedantic curate is called Sir Nathaniel, 'Sir' being a courtesy title for priests.

clue.text: Is study included in symbols?

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: to con is to study or learn

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether learning counts among a set of emblems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'included in' is the container signal; 'study' in the sense of learning by heart is an old meaning of the verb con.
explanation.definitionFit: Icons are images standing for something else, a kind of emblem.

clue.text: Trademark: Greek maiden seen in unconscious drawing

indicators.note: the maiden is seen inside the other pieces

parts.note: the id is the unconscious part of the psyche in Freud
a graph is a drawn diagram
Io was the maiden loved by Zeus in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A Greek girl appears in a sketch made without thinking, which becomes a brand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' is the container signal; 'unconscious' reads as an adjective but stands for Freud's noun, the id.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiograph is a private mark or signature, hence a trade mark.

clue.text: US novelist suggests protection for conqueror and queen

parts.note: the Normans conquered England in 1066
mail is chain armour
ER is the abbreviation for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: An American writer proposes armour for a conqueror and his queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in clue order: NORMAN, then MAIL, then ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Mailer wrote The Naked and the Dead and many other American novels.

clue.text: Lawrentian flute symbolically broken

parts.note: in a D. H. Lawrence novel the hero's flute, named after the biblical rod that blossomed, is smashed as a symbol

explanation.surface: A musical instrument in a Lawrence novel is broken as a symbol.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lawrence's Aaron's Rod, Aaron Sisson's flute (the 'rod') is smashed near the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title names the flute itself, after the biblical staff that budded.

clue.text: "With an old horse that — and nods" (Hardy)

definitions.text: "With an old horse that — and nods" (Hardy)

parts.words: "With an old horse that — and nods" (Hardy)
parts.note: a missing word from Hardy's poem 'In Time of "The Breaking of Nations"', describing a weary horse that trips

explanation.surface: A line of Hardy's poetry with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem opens: 'Only a man harrowing clods / In a slow silent walk / With an old horse that stumbles and nods'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means trips or loses footing, as an old horse does.

clue.text: Severe Jamesian father, with the heart of a Trollopian chaplain

definitions.text: Severe Jamesian father, with the heart of a Trollopian chaplain

parts.words: Severe Jamesian father, with the heart of a Trollopian chaplain
parts.note: the stern father in Henry James's Washington Square has a name whose middle is the name of Trollope's oily chaplain in Barchester Towers

explanation.surface: A stern father from Henry James is said to have a Trollope clergyman's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Sloper of Washington Square contains SLOPE, Mr Slope being the bishop's chaplain in Barchester Towers.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Austin Sloper is the cold, forbidding father of Catherine in James's Washington Square.

clue.text: Chekhovian protagonists in novel by May Sinclair recalling the Brontës

definitions.text: novel by May Sinclair recalling the Brontës

explanation.surface: Chekhov's characters appear in a novel echoing the Brontë family.
explanation.walkthrough: Chekhov's play and May Sinclair's 1914 novel, modelled on the Brontës, share the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov's play centres on Olga, Masha and Irina; Sinclair's novel follows three Brontë-like daughters of a vicar.

clue.text: Similarly cosy, but pullulating, like William Adamson's formicarium

parts.note: as means in the same way
warm means snug and cosy

explanation.surface: An ant colony in a novel is called both snug and teeming.
explanation.walkthrough: William Adamson is the naturalist hero of A. S. Byatt's 'Morpho Eugenia' (Angels and Insects), who keeps a glass ants' nest.
explanation.definitionFit: Pullulating means teeming with life, like an ants' nest crowded with insects.

clue.text: Concerning black French painter and…

parts.note: re means about or concerning
noir is the French word for black

explanation.surface: A remark about a dark French artist, continued into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 22-down, the father and son both being Renoirs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was the Impressionist painter of Le Déjeuner des canotiers.

clue.text: Distorted, mad morale seen in Sweeney Todd, say

indicators.note: distorted means twisted out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Warped and angry spirits are found in the barber of Fleet Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distorted' rearranges MAD MORALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeney Todd began as a Victorian sensational stage thriller, a classic example of the genre.

clue.text: … much the same again

parts.note: following on from the painter, this asks for the word used to say the same thing once more

explanation.surface: Completing the previous clue: the painter, and then more of the same.
explanation.walkthrough: Read with 20-down: Renoir and his son, the film-maker Jean, a second Renoir.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is used to repeat what was just said, meaning the same once more.

clue.text: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring

definitions.text: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring

parts.words: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring
parts.note: an Elizabethan pamphleteer wrote Lenten Stuffe in praise of the red herring of Great Yarmouth

explanation.surface: A writer's Lent fare turns out to be a smoked fish, or a false trail.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Nashe's Lenten Stuffe (1599) is a mock encomium of the Yarmouth red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Nashe wrote that pamphlet praising the smoked fish of Yarmouth.

clue.text: Swift glimpse of island in flight

definitions.text: Swift glimpse of island in flight

parts.words: Swift glimpse of island in flight
parts.note: in Gulliver's Travels Jonathan Swift describes a flying island

explanation.surface: A quick sight of an island passing overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' looks like 'quick' but is Jonathan Swift, whose Gulliver sees the flying island of Laputa.
explanation.definitionFit: Laputa is the airborne island visited by Gulliver in Swift's satire.

clue.text: Italian painter in wild rigadoon

indicators.note: a wild dance suggests the letters of the word are thrown about

explanation.surface: An Italian artist joins in a frenzied old dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges RIGADOON, a lively Baroque dance. Luca Giordano was a Neapolitan Baroque painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Luca Giordano was a prolific seventeenth-century Neapolitan painter.

clue.text: Namely poor, and backward, he survived four of The Histories

definitions.text: he survived four of The Histories

parts.note: sc. (scilicet) means namely

indicators.note: backward means the word poor is read from the end

explanation.surface: A poor and slow character outlasts several history plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns POOR into ROOP. A Scroop appears in Richard II, both parts of Henry IV and Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Scroop family appear across four of Shakespeare's history plays.
